title: Visiting the sick
hookLine: the Talmud says a visitor takes away a sixtieth of the illness (Nedarim 39b)

cards: One sixtieth. That's the claim in the Talmud, tractate Nedarim: whoever visits a sick person takes away a sixtieth of the illness. The rabbis around the table do the math out loud.
Then sixty visitors should cure him completely? They don't laugh it off, and they don't take it literally. They add conditions and keep going.
Nobody in the conversation says the visit is pointless. The argument is only about how much it carries.

teach.b: In Hebrew it's bikur cholim, visiting the sick, and you met it in your first year at Abraham's tent. There Abraham is recovering from his circumcision, and the text says the Lord appeared to him.

The Talmud reads that as God visiting the sick, and draws a line: as God visits the sick, so should you. Visiting is walking in God's ways. On the same page in Nedarim, a student of Rabbi Akiva falls ill and nobody comes.
Akiva goes himself. The floor is swept and sprinkled for the sick man, he recovers, and the student says, Rabbi, you have brought me back to life.
Akiva walks out and teaches: anyone who does not visit the sick is like one who sheds blood. Strong words, to make a point: absence costs something. Later teachers give practical advice.
Don't stay so long you exhaust the person. Sit at their level, not looming over the bed. Ask what they need: the floor swept, the groceries, the dog walked.
And pray while you're there, the tradition says, because you see their need with your own eyes.
There's a short line people say: may God have mercy on you among all the sick of Israel.
Even the prayer refuses to leave anyone alone.
A sixtieth is small. It is not nothing.

how: Visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is a commandment and an act of kindness in Jewish life; some synagogues have a bikur cholim group that organizes visits, calls, meals and errands for members who are ill or homebound.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is sick or stuck at home right now, and picture where they are sitting today.
Ask what they might need that isn't advice, and plan a visit, small and real: a call, a doorstep drop-off, a short visit in a low chair. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Visiting the sick. Bikur cholim: the way God visited Abraham, Akiva at a lonely student's bedside, a short visit, and a prayer at the bedside. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: visiting lightens. Showing up, even briefly, carries more than it seems. Until tomorrow.
